analysis.title: The 60/40 Portfolio Is Caught In An Inflation Trap
key_insights: Treasuries are losing value as an equity hedge in 60/40 portfolios because inflation has returned to a persistently elevated regime.

When 10-year yields stay above 5.25%-5.50%, the stock-bond correlation has almost always been positive, so stocks and Treasuries can fall together. The correlation was mostly negative from 2000 to 2020, which made Treasuries a good hedge.
60/40 and risk-parity strategies together hold roughly $1.5 trillion of Treasuries. If the correlation stays positive, hedging demand for Treasuries is likely to weaken.

Risk-parity funds' sensitivity to Treasuries (controlling for stocks) has fallen to 15-year lows over the last two years, even as the stock-bond correlation has been rising. This suggests the funds have sensed a regime change.
The shift is self-reinforcing. Lower Treasury demand reduces liquidity and raises term premium, which supports yields and keeps the stock-bond correlation positive.
Inflation, not yields, drives the correlation. The stock-bond correlation has almost always been positive when core PCE is above 3%.
3% has historically been where inflation shifts non-linearly. A 2016 Fed paper says a stable inflation regime is hard to maintain at an average level much above 3%.

Inflation shocks tend to mean-revert when core PCE is below 2%. When inflation is high, past inflation feeds into expectations and shocks become cumulative, making price pressures more persistent and more volatile.

Internet searches on inflation rise markedly above about 3.5% headline CPI (consistent with 3% core PCE), so attention and expectation anchoring change above that level. This leaves the Fed less room to cut rates.
With less room to cut, bonds move less inversely to stocks in a slowdown, and the correlation moves back toward its typical positive state seen over most of the past 120 years.
Core PCE is back above 3% and has averaged just below 3% over the last 12 months, so the author sees poor prospects for escaping the high-inflation regime that has persisted for most of this decade.

Above this yield range the stock-bond correlation has almost always been positive. 3% core PCE has historically coincided with a 10-year yield around 5.25%.

Reduced Treasury hedging demand lowers liquidity and raises term premium, which supports yields.
